source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: Founding design of CYRUS. Events are stored in Episodic Memory Organization Packets (E-MOPs). Each E-MOP holds generalized norms plus an index tree that separates events by how they differ from the norms. Retrieval builds and elaborates a search context instead of scanning a category.
numbers: Domain: events in the lives of Secretaries of State Vance and Muskie. 247-page report. About 10 search strategies; 3 MOP classes (scripts, simple MOPs, intentional MOPs); 9 scripts, 10 simple MOPs, 4 intentional MOPs in the full E-MOP list.
quote: A few powerful strategies for search, combined with rich conceptual indexing, allow retrieval without category enumeration.
limits: Hand-built domain knowledge for one narrow domain. No quantitative accuracy test; evaluation is by worked examples.
agent_relevance: Direct blueprint for a case memory: a few generalized nodes with discriminating indices, not a flat list of past episodes.

source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: Design requirement: retrieval time should not grow as memory grows. Kolodner states the psychology debate openly: the fan effect says retrieval slows with more facts, but context-guided retrieval need not.
numbers: Cites Anderson 1974/1976 (fan effect), Smith, Adams & Schorr 1978 (no slowdown when context guides retrieval), Reder & Anderson 1980 (no interference for consistency judgments).
limits: The no-slowdown claim was a design goal, not measured in CYRUS with a growing store. Psychology evidence was mixed even then.
agent_relevance: Memory size scaling is the central worry for an agent that keeps every episode. Index by differences, not by enumeration, to keep lookup cheap.

source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: Generalization rule in CYRUS: the first two events that share an index form a new E-MOP, and the features they share become provisional norms. Certainty of each norm rises with confirming events and falls with conflicting ones. Bad early generalizations are removed later.
numbers: Certainty is not evaluated until an E-MOP holds 6 events. Sub-MOPs that index a large majority of the parent's events are collapsed into the parent. Example: 'trips to the Middle East include a state dinner' is dropped if later trips lack one.
limits: The 6-event value is an implementation detail the author calls stabilizing, not an empirically fitted number. 'Large majority' is not given as a number.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete rule for when a lesson drawn from two episodes may be trusted: wait for more cases, track counter-evidence, and be able to retract.

source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: Index control prevents memory blow-up. Only salient, domain-relevant features become indices. A feature true of almost all events stays a norm and is not indexed. A feature kept as an index must show predictive power.
numbers: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) later note CYRUS allows only a small vocabulary of indices to avoid explosive index growth.
limits: Index vocabulary was chosen by hand for the diplomat domain.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold: index lessons by the features that differ from the usual case, and cap the index vocabulary.

source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: Generalized knowledge and episodes live in the same structure, so retrieving a general fact uses the same process as retrieving one event. Kolodner argues this supports no sharp episodic vs semantic split.
numbers: Example queries that need only E-MOP norms: where Vance usually stays on trips; whether welcome ceremonies usually have parades.
limits: Claimed as an easy extension, not demonstrated in the thesis.
agent_relevance: A memory that answers 'what usually happens' without replaying cases is cheaper than replaying all similar cases.

source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: Retrieval failure is predicted by encoding specificity: an event is found only through features it was discriminated on at the time of retrieval, so cues must be transformed or elaborated into indexed features.
numbers: Predicted relation: closer cue-to-encoding match means easier retrieval. Memory reorganizes over time, so the indices at retrieval time, not at input time, decide ease.
limits: Prediction stated, not tested in the thesis. Tulving 1972 is the cited human basis.
agent_relevance: Query rewriting to match how a lesson was indexed is a principled retrieval step; a bad cue means a miss even if the case exists.

source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: CYRUS answers questions by (1) picking a MOP by schema triggering, (2) building a search key by inference, (3) searching related events. About 10 search strategies were modelled on strategies seen in people.
numbers: CyFr (CYRUS plus FRUMP) had processed about 50 stories on Vance and about 30 on Muskie at the time of the thesis (the Dec 1980 CyFr report says about 10 on Muskie).
limits: Story counts differ between two Yale reports written weeks apart. System ran on a few dozen stories, so scale tests were never done.
agent_relevance: Shows the early ceiling: tens of cases, hand-coded structure. Do not assume the architecture was shown to scale.

source: Kolodner (1980) Retrieval and organizational strategies in conceptual memory: a computer model (Yale RR-187, PhD thesis)
finding: Kolodner compares CYRUS with Lebowitz's concurrent IPP. Both use MOPs to organize episodes and build generalizations. IPP emphasizes using generalizations to understand later stories; CYRUS emphasizes retrieving episodes.
numbers: IPP example from the thesis: after many Italian kidnapping stories with businessmen victims, IPP infers an unnamed victim in a later story is probably a businessman.
limits: Description of IPP here is second-hand from a rival author. Lebowitz's own reports were not found open.
agent_relevance: Generalizations built from stored cases can fill missing details in new cases; also a source of confident wrong defaults.

source: Schank, Kolodner & DeJong (1980) Conceptual information retrieval (Yale RR-190)
finding: Describes CyFr: FRUMP reads UPI news and sends summaries to CYRUS, which files them in memory and answers English questions. The paper states the rule for splitting categories: deviations from the norm make good sub-categories, norms do not.
numbers: FRUMP: about 60 sketchy scripts, about 2300 root words, about 8.5 s CPU for a sample article, said to keep up with the UPI wire in real time. CyFr had about 50 Vance stories and about 10 Muskie stories.
quote: Thus, norms are not good category specifiers, but deviations from a norm are good.
limits: System-description paper. No accuracy numbers, no user study. Hand-built scripts.
agent_relevance: Early example of an automatic write path (read text, summarize, file into organized memory) feeding a read path.

source: Schank, Kolodner & DeJong (1980) Conceptual information retrieval (Yale RR-190)
finding: Hand-coded vs machine-coded input exposed a gap. Hand-coded events named their E-MOPs and implied related events. FRUMP's output did not, so a separate program (CYRECV) had to infer the E-MOP and the related trips and negotiations.
numbers: Qualitative; one worked example (Vance in Madrid story, June 1980), described in the thesis chapter 8.
limits: Reported as a design problem, not as a measured error rate.
agent_relevance: The write path needs inference to attach the right context to a raw episode; raw summaries alone index badly.

source: Schank (1979) Reminding and memory organization: an introduction to MOPs (Yale RR-170)
finding: Starting point of dynamic memory. Bower, Black & Turner (1979) found people confuse stories about a dentist and a doctor, which a single restaurant-style script cannot explain. Schank replaces monolithic scripts with smaller shared scenes and MOPs that tie scenes together.
numbers: Report is 97 pages, Dec 1979. Two predicted confusion types: links between scenes interpreted by different structures break; details inside a script get normalized, except very weird deviations.
quote: a more fragmented, multi-level set of memory structures (MOPs), which are more flexible than scripts
limits: No new experiment. Human data comes from Bower, Black & Turner 1979 and Owens, Bower & Black (1978), cited but not opened here.
agent_relevance: Memory units should be small and shareable, so lessons transfer across surface-different tasks; the cost is more cross-task confusion.

source: Schank (1979) Reminding and memory organization: an introduction to MOPs (Yale RR-170)
finding: Reminding mechanism: a script runs scene by scene. When an event deviates from the script's expectation, the scene becomes an entry point into memories hung off that scene, so a past episode is recalled exactly when the current one violates the same expectation.
numbers: Example: restaurant ordering scene with four stored deviations (e.g., banging silverware to get service).
limits: Mechanism is a theory with anecdotal examples. Schank also notes the most appropriate reminding feels least like reminding.
agent_relevance: Retrieval triggered by expectation failure, not by surface similarity. Matches guardrail G1 (act on a signal, not on a schedule).

source: Bower, Black & Turner (1979) Scripts in memory for text
finding: Human experiments on script-based text memory that found recognition confusions between stories of different but similar script types (dentist vs doctor). This is the main human data the MOP theory was built to explain.
numbers: No numbers recorded; known only through Schank's 1979 report.
limits: Not opened this session. Details must be checked in the original (Cognitive Psychology, 1979) before citing numbers.
agent_relevance: Source of the human-confusion claim; check before citing numbers.

source: Kolodner & Barsalou (c. 1981-82) Psychological issues raised by an AI model of reconstructive memory (Cognitive Science Society proceedings)
finding: A psychologist and the model's author list the open human-data questions that CYRUS raises: are events the basic organizing unit, do people elaborate cues as CYRUS does, how is a discriminating feature chosen, is generic structure acquired automatically or by attention.
numbers: No data. Plans experiments. Cites Williams & Hollan (1981) as the existing human evidence for elaboration strategies in retrieval from very long-term memory.
limits: Position paper; the authors say the model was incomplete and gaps were filled on the basis of intuition. OCR text was partly garbled, so details beyond the main claims are unverified. Year is approximate.
agent_relevance: Honest labelling: the E-MOP design is a theory with weak human validation. Treat it as an engineering pattern, not a proven model of the mind.

source: Kolodner & Barsalou (c. 1981-82) Psychological issues raised by an AI model of reconstructive memory (Cognitive Science Society proceedings)
finding: Compact statement of E-MOP update: when a new episode is indexed identically to an old one, a new E-MOP forms, norms are the shared features, indices are the differences. Later episodes refine the norms. A feature that was an index can become a norm, and a false norm can be demoted to an index.
numbers: Retrieval model: a request must name an E-MOP and indices; an index cannot be traversed unless the cue specifies it. Three repair strategies: schema triggering, inferring plausible index values, and using related events.
limits: Described, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Both promotion (index to norm) and demotion (norm to index) are needed so memory can fix its own early mistakes.

source: Dehn (1981) Memory in story invention (Yale, AUTHOR program)
finding: Applies CYRUS-style reconstructive retrieval to creative generation: inventing a story is memory search run on a goal. Reminding is expected to supply useful ideas when indexing is rich, and search proceeds by successive reformulation of a partial answer.
numbers: Worked example of CYRUS: asked if Vance's wife met Mrs. Begin, CYRUS answered 'at a state dinner in Israel' by inferring where such a meeting would be stored. No quantitative evaluation.
limits: Program under development at the time of writing; no results reported. OCR text is rough. Year is approximate.
agent_relevance: Link to generation: retrieval-by-reformulation is a way to turn a vague goal into a concrete memory probe.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1)
finding: Standard formal summary of the dynamic memory model. A generalized episode (GE) holds norms (features common to all its cases), indices (features that discriminate its cases) and cases. Retrieval finds the GE with most shared norms, then follows indices to the case matching most remaining features.
numbers: Calls CYRUS the first system that may be called a case-based reasoner. Notes the discrimination-network index may grow explosively; CYRUS limits indices to a small vocabulary.
quote: Norms are features common to all cases indexed under a GE. Indices are features which discriminate between a GE's cases.
limits: Review, not original data. The authors flag their 'most features in common' criterion as illustrative only.
agent_relevance: Clean abstraction for implementing the memory: norms, indices, cases, plus a rule that two cases on the same index spawn a new GE.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1)
finding: Contrasts the dynamic memory model with the category-exemplar model of PROTOS. Notes CYRUS-type systems retrieve on surface (syntactic) similarity, whereas PROTOS, CASEY, GREBE and CREEK use deeper knowledge-based similarity.
numbers: The review calls the dynamic memory a plausible, although simplified, model of human reasoning and learning.
limits: Plausibility claim is by the review authors, not backed by new tests.
agent_relevance: Surface-similarity retrieval is a known weakness of the early line; later knowledge-intensive matching responded to it.

source: Wikipedia: Case-based reasoning
finding: CBR traces to Schank and students at Yale in the early 1980s. Schank's dynamic memory model was the basis for the first CBR systems, Kolodner's CYRUS and Lebowitz's IPP.
numbers: Cited papers: Schank 1982 Dynamic Memory (Cambridge UP); Kolodner 1983 Reconstructive memory: a computer model, Cognitive Science 7; Lebowitz 1983 Memory-based parsing, Artificial Intelligence 21, pp 363-404.
limits: Encyclopedia summary; page does not mention MOPs or Abelson.
agent_relevance: Confirms the lineage the agent's memory design borrows from.

source: Watson (course slides) CBR 1, Univ. of Auckland
finding: Timeline slide: 1977 scripts (Schank, Abelson); 1983 dynamic memory and MOPs; 1984 CYRUS as first implemented CBR system; 1984-88 JUDGE, SWALE, CHEF, JULIA. Rationale for indexing differences between cases.
numbers: Dates only. Slide dating of CYRUS (1984) differs from the 1983 journal paper and 1980 thesis.
limits: Teaching slides; date of CYRUS varies by source (1978 first report, 1980 thesis, 1983 papers, 1984 book). Slide year approximate.
agent_relevance: Use primary reports for dates when writing the schema notes.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs (arXiv 2508.16153)
finding: Casts an LLM agent as a memory-based decision process with a case bank. A GPT-4.1 planner retrieves past cases (state, action, reward) by SimCSE cosine similarity, or by a learned Q-function, and an o3 / o4-mini executor acts. No weight updates.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3 (L1 96.23, L2 90.70, L3 61.54); GAIA test 79.40% (4th); DeepResearcher avg 66.6 F1 and 80.4 PM; HLE 24.4 PM vs GPT-5 25.32; SimpleQA 95.0%.
limits: GAIA validation used 3 iterations on the same validation set; test used the bank built on validation. Many other strong components (tools, planner, executor). Case memory is one factor, not isolated in the headline numbers.
agent_relevance: Closest modern descendant of the dynamic-memory line, but it uses a flat bank with embedding retrieval, not a MOP hierarchy.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs (arXiv 2508.16153)
finding: Ablation on the number of retrieved cases: a handful helps, more does not. Authors conclude case memory benefits from a small high-quality set, unlike many-shot prompting.
quote: CBR benefits from a small, high-quality memory
limits: Single benchmark family; K=0 still keeps planner and tools. Plateau after K=4.
agent_relevance: Retrieve few cases (about 4), not many. More cases add cost without gain.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs (arXiv 2508.16153)
finding: Learning-curve ablation separates the part due to cases from the part due to repeated attempts. Over five iterations, the no-CBR variant also climbs a lot; the extra gain from CBR is small.
numbers: DeepResearcher accuracy iter1 to iter5: w/o CBR 78.65 to 84.47; non-parametric CBR 79.84 to 84.85; parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44. CBR adds 1.2-1.8 points at iter1 and 0.4-1.0 at iter5. Abstract claims +4.7 to +9.6 on out-of-distribution tasks.
limits: No variance or seeds reported in the table. Gains in the in-distribution loop are under 2 points, so noise could matter.
agent_relevance: Honest read: much of the learning is repetition and tool use. Test memory against a no-memory control with the same retries.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: case-based reasoning for RAG in LLMs for legal QA (arXiv 2404.04302)
finding: Uses the CBR retrieve step to build the LLM prompt. Cases are question, support, answer tuples with extracted entities. Hybrid weighted similarity over three embeddings (question, support, answer) is compared with BERT, LegalBERT and AnglE-BERT.
numbers: Case base 2,084 cases (from 2,124 Australian legal QA pairs, 40 removed). Test set 32 questions. Generator Mistral-7B. Cosine to reference answer: No-RAG 0.8967; best hybrid AnglE-BERT k=3 full case 0.9141 (+1.94%). Significant vs No-RAG at 95% (one-tailed t-test), vs hybrid BERT k=1 at 90%.
limits: Tiny test set (32), synthetic QA from GPT-4, similarity to reference by embedding cosine not human or exact-match grading, high baseline of 0.8967. Effect is small.
agent_relevance: Structured, multi-field case retrieval beat plain retrieval only slightly on this task; do not expect large gains from case structure alone.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (AAAI; arXiv 2308.10144)
finding: Two memory modes together: retrieve similar successful trajectories (episodic) and extract natural-language insights by comparing success/failure pairs (generalized norms). Insight list is edited with ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE; an insight is dropped when its importance count reaches zero.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: 36% vs 31% (HotpotQA) and 50% vs 55% (ALFWorld). ALFWorld 54% at Reflexion round 3 vs 59% for ExpeL; HotpotQA 40% vs 39%. HotpotQA ablation: ReAct 28.0, ExpeL 39.0.
limits: Numbers read from ablation tables and text; the main bar chart has no printed values. Small test sets, GPT-3.5/4 era.
agent_relevance: Same split as E-MOPs: case store plus a maintained list of norms with votes. Insights helped reasoning tasks, cases helped action-sequence tasks.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL (ablations)
finding: Retrieval basis matters. Retrieving by task similarity beat retrieving by reasoning similarity and clearly beat random selection. Insights extracted from the given few-shot examples alone gave no gain over ReAct, so real experience is needed. Adding reflections to insight extraction hurt.
numbers: ALFWorld: random-sampled examples 40.0%; task-similarity (ExpeL) 59.0%; reasoning-similarity in between (table layout garbled, exact value uncertain). HotpotQA: ExpeL 39.0 vs 29.0 for a variant with reflections in insight extraction (row pairing uncertain).
limits: Table layout was garbled in text extraction; row pairings for some values are uncertain.
agent_relevance: Pick cases by task similarity, and do not feed self-reflections into the general lesson list.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent workflow memory (arXiv 2409.07429)
finding: Induces reusable workflows (generalized routines) from past trajectories and supplies them to the agent, offline or online. Closest LLM analogue of a MOP: a shared sub-routine abstracted from several episodes.
numbers: WebArena total success 35.5% vs 23.5% BrowserGym baseline (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative); Mind2Web cross-task step success +24.6% relative; online AWM gains of 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test gap widens; about 2.0 fewer steps per example.
limits: GPT-4 at temperature 0; WebArena has no train split so workflows come from test queries online (no held-out proof). Text table garbled, so per-site numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Abstracting a routine from several cases transfers across tasks and websites better than raw cases.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank (arXiv 2509.25140)
finding: Distills strategy-level memory items from both successes and failures, judged by an LLM judge, and compares with raw-trajectory memory (Synapse) and success-only workflows (AWM).
numbers: WebArena overall success with Gemini-2.5-flash: No memory 40.5; Synapse 42.1; AWM 44.1; ReasoningBank 48.8; plus parallel test-time scaling 51.8. Steps 9.7 down to 8.3. Up to 20% relative gain, 16% fewer steps claimed. Shopping subset: AWM drops 44.4 to 42.2 when failures are added; ReasoningBank rises 46.5 to 49.7.
limits: Some memory baselines gave under 2 points over no memory in this setup. Judge accuracy was only 72.7%, yet results held from 90% to 70% simulated judge accuracy. Authors are the method's proposers.
agent_relevance: Failures are a usable memory source if abstracted into lessons; raw failed trajectories are noise.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet (arXiv 2504.07952)
finding: Test-time memory that rewrites a short cheatsheet after each problem, with optional retrieval and synthesis (DC-RS). No ground-truth labels needed.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23% to 50%; GPT-4o Game of 24 10% to 99% (DC-RS, by reusing a stored Python solution); GPQA-Diamond +9%; MMLU-Pro Eng/Physics up to +8%.
limits: Largest gains come from storing one reusable code snippet, which suits repeating task types. AIME 2024 has 30 questions so one problem is 3.3 points.
agent_relevance: Gains are largest when the same method recurs; expect little where tasks do not repeat.

source: Sumers et al. (2024) CoALA: cognitive architectures for language agents (TMLR; arXiv 2309.02427)
finding: Frames language agents with working memory plus episodic, semantic and procedural long-term stores. Episodic stores earlier decision-cycle experience; semantic facts may come from reflection on episodes.
numbers: No benchmark numbers. Notes writing to procedural memory is riskier than writing to episodic or semantic memory because it can introduce bugs.
limits: Conceptual survey.
agent_relevance: Gives vocabulary mapping E-MOP style memory onto agent design: episodes in episodic store, norms in semantic store.

source: Xu et al. (2025) A-Mem: agentic memory for LLM agents (arXiv 2502.12110)
finding: Each new memory becomes a note with context, keywords, tags and links to similar notes, and old notes can be rewritten when new ones arrive. This echoes MOP reorganization but is LLM-driven.
numbers: LoCoMo (7,512 QA, avg 9K-token dialogues): about 1,200 tokens per memory operation vs about 16,900 for LoCoMo and MemGPT baselines (85-93% fewer tokens). DialSim F1 3.45 vs 2.55 (LoCoMo) and 1.18 (MemGPT).
limits: Absolute F1 values are low (3.45 on DialSim); gains are relative. Baselines are those the authors chose.
agent_relevance: Dynamic re-linking can cut tokens; no test of whether re-linking itself causes the accuracy gain.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Case-based or rule-based: how do transformers do the math? (ICML; arXiv 2402.17709)
finding: Tests whether transformers reason by rules or by similar seen cases. In leave-square-out tests on addition, models trained on over 95% of the pairs get 100% on random splits but fail on held-out squares far from training data, so they behave case-based.
numbers: Random split: 100% accuracy. Leave-square-out: holes in accuracy away from the training boundary. Fix: Rule-Following Fine-Tuning lets models trained on 1-5 digit addition reach over 95% on 12-digit addition, over 40 points above scratchpad.
limits: Fine-tuned GPT-2 and Llama-2-7B on arithmetic tasks, not prompting of frontier models. Arithmetic only.
agent_relevance: Case-like behavior in a model is a weakness for out-of-range inputs; a scaffold must supply rules when cases do not cover the problem.
